findings.defect: Item 3's comb is still in the 1440p animated frames. Every cloud in and near the glint trails a curtain of fine vertical streaks, 1-3 px wide and 30-80 px long, running down-screen along the sun's azimuth. They cross the bright glint and the cloud tops next to them, so the field looks like dripping paint or rain smeared on a lens. Single dark blue-grey specks sit in the glint, e.g. (1327, 781) = (146, 167, 197) against 216-231 around it, and (1366, 857). Seen at full frame, the glint is a striated smear. The sunset view from the ground no longer shows any of this.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/earth-orbit-clouds/cloud-shadows-sunset-tanzania.jpg and glint-clouds-south-america.jpg: shadows at low sun are long, straight, smooth-edged lanes many cloud heights long. They taper and fade with distance as haze fills them, and they show no internal striation. Clouds over a glint are clean dark silhouettes, and their shadows cut clean offset holes in the glint.
findings.likelyCause: The 3x3 / 7x3 tent of cloudShadowFilter widens the map ACROSS the sun's azimuth only. Along the azimuth, a low-sun texel is still stretched many times on the ground, and the map's per-texel quantisation shows as streaks along that direction. The hand-off also says the ocean's forward surface still reads the map by hand (ocean-cs-2): the glint may read the unfiltered map, which would explain why the streaks are strongest on the sea. On cloud tops, the streaks point to the map term the cloud march adds beyond its 2.5 km cone.
findings.fixDirection: Filter along the sun's azimuth too, with a penumbra that grows with distance from the occluder (PCSS style, sun angular radius), or march the true sun direction with jittered samples below about 8 deg. Make the ocean read the filtered map (follow ocean-cs-2 with the ocean owner). Add a spec on native-leo-low-sun: the ratio of high-frequency energy across the azimuth to energy along it, inside the glint, must not exceed that of the open sea.

findings.view: Whole-disc Earth: C:\dev\fable-space-game\out\screens\atmosphere\native-earth-60000km-1440p.png (x 1150-1650, y 520-900 native), perf-60-000-km-1440p.png, explore\m-14000km-1080p.png (x 700-1200, y 420-720), explore\m-20000km-1080p.png, earth-moon-distance.png (x 560-800, y 220-460), earth-60000km.png, earth-60000km-crescent.png
findings.defect: Inside systems, the 60,000 km disc has more tones than in round 0, but two procedural signatures now give it away. (1) Every stretch of open ocean is covered with a uniform two-tone camouflage of pale-blue rounded cells, the same size everywhere and with no direction. At 14,000-20,000 km it covers half the disc like leopard print (m-14000km crop). (2) Cloud edges are stair-stepped in 2-4 px blocks. Each has a bright white rim and a darker line inside it, so the clouds read as embossed plaster or a bas-relief, not vapour. Near the terminator the edges become red-brown hairline outlines with dark interiors. This is what the player sees for the whole lunar transfer, and in the map view.
findings.realReference: Apollo 17 Blue Marble and DSCOVR EPIC whole-disc frames (and earth-orbit-clouds/cloud-gazing-pacific.jpg at closer range): thin cloud over the ocean is fibrous streaks, speckled cumulus fields and veils, organised along fronts and trade winds, never a uniform cell print. Cloud edges at 10-25 km per pixel are soft, graded transmittance with no bright rim and no relief shading except long shadows right at the terminator. At the terminator the tops turn pink-orange over hundreds of km.
findings.likelyCause: (1) The thin fair-weather fields the model adds where the map's coverage is low are made from the mesoscale Worley cells (one octave, one cell size). Their opacity mottling survives at this footprint, while the map itself is flat inside systems (request atmosphere-clouds-8, open). (2) The 'mesoscale relief shading' of round-1 part 3 shades by a cloud-top gradient whose texel is several km, which embosses every coverage edge. The tile march's four rays per pixel do not anti-alias a hard opacity threshold at the map's finest level. At the terminator, only the thin edges are dim enough to show the reddened sun.
findings.fixDirection: Fade the relief shading out by footprint (no relief term once a texel exceeds about 2 km) or limit it to the terminator band, where low sun makes relief visible. Replace the isotropic Worley thin-cloud field at these footprints with an anisotropic, multi-octave field aligned with the map's flow (or drop it beyond about 5 km per pixel and let the map carry thin cloud). Soften the coverage-to-opacity transfer into a ramp over at least one map texel. Filter the tile result transmittance-aware. Add a spec: the open-ocean variance in the 60,000 km and 14,000 km frames stays under a bound, and no bright rim exceeds the cloud interior along the edges.

findings.defect: The contour lines are gone, but a deck still looks like cloud from only one distance (about 6 km). (a) From 25 km, at sun 50 deg, the deck is a flat two-tone camouflage of hard-edged pale patches on grey, with no relief or shading (tunables-shipped sd 5.6 over the lower half). At sun 10 deg it is uniform khaki sand (148, 139, 130) with blotches and navy pits, like a beach with seaweed, not a deck in golden low light. (b) From 400 km it is a uniform light-grey card (187, 185, 184), sd 3.3, sprinkled with thin pale worm-like squiggles. (c) From below, the base is overlapping smooth grey lobes with crisp outlines, like layered paper cut-outs, plus a faint pink arc at the top right. (d) From 6 km in animated mode the deck is credible at a glance, but at 1:1 it reads as crumpled foil or snowfield: craggy facets and dark crevasses instead of rounded billows.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/earth-orbit-clouds/stratocumulus-field.jpg: km-size closed cells organised in rolls, bright cells (p95 Y 0.54) with darker gaps (about 7x), texture at many scales, merging smoothly toward the horizon. sky-ground-clouds/sc-lacunosus-stormy.jpg and overcast-landscape.jpg from below: soft mottling (p95/p5 1.8x for a flat overcast, 6.9x for a lacunosus), rows and cells, no cut-out outlines. sky-ground-clouds/cu-from-airliner-10km.jpg: rounded heaps with soft blue shade.
findings.likelyCause: The deck has no cell structure of its own. Beyond the shape noise's useful footprint, what shows is the mesoscale Worley cell channel thresholded into fraction (the camouflage) and its cell edges (the worms). The relief is a smooth bell profile with shape-noise relief carved in, and the light samples see little of it at 25 km, so the top is unshaded. At sun 10 deg the colour is the reddened direct term with almost no cool sky fill. From below, the base is the shape field's surface with no internal density variation, so lobe outlines stay hard.
findings.fixDirection: Give stratiform cloud a closed-cell height and density field (Worley cells 0.7-2 km, several octaves, domain-warped), with opacity dips at cell edges and relief that both the eye march and the light march resolve, kept consistent across footprints by a mip-consistent baked field. Light the shaded side with the sky dome away from the sun (as done for cumulus in item 10). From below, modulate base brightness by the optical depth above, plus mottling. Specs: the deck's high-pass energy from 25 km stays within a band of the 6 km value, scaled for distance; at sun 10 deg the cell tops are warm against cool shadows.

findings.view: Night side at a dark-adapted exposure: C:\dev\fable-space-game\out\screens\atmosphere\leo-night-airglow.png (whole lower half; band x 0-1280, y 340-430)
findings.defect: NEW. With the sun 40 deg below the horizon, the surface below the airglow is lit saturated royal blue: the deck on the left is (47, 63, 140) to (63, 83, 156). It is brighter than the airglow band (55, 66, 30), and rust-brown smears lie across it. The broken field on the right is bright blue lumps over black. The frame looks like a day scene through a blue 'day-for-night' filter, not a night photograph. The airglow is a uniform olive-drab tube about 25 px tall with hard top and bottom edges. The red layer above it is a broad dim maroon haze about 70 px tall, not a thin red shell.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/earth-orbit-clouds/limb-panorama.jpg: night Earth Y about 0.015, faint green-brown; airglow peak Y 0.16, (91, 106, 75), thin, sharp-edged on top, fading below within about 3 % of the frame height; the band is the brightest thing on the night side. airglow-red-yellow.jpg: moonlit clouds visible but low contrast and NEUTRAL grey (110, 112, 117), median scene Y 0.014; a thin yellow-green shell with red just above it.
findings.likelyCause: Some ambient term lights the clouds and ground on the night side with a blue colour and far too much intensity relative to the airglow: the sky-irradiance table's residual at deep negative sun, a night or starlight floor in the cloud ambient, or moon or planetshine with a blue cast. It is amplified about 14 stops by EV -5. The source has to be traced in the cloud lighting (cloudMarchFsWgsl ambient) and in the core's night ambient. The olive band suggests the 557.7 nm emission is mapped to sRGB without the other emissions of the band and with a low blue channel. The broad maroon haze suggests too large a scale height for the red 630 nm layer.
findings.fixDirection: Debug-print the night-side cloud and ground luminance by term (sun multi-scatter, irradiance table, ambient floor, moon). With no moon, the night surface must sit about an order of magnitude below the airglow band. Moonlight, when present, must be neutral and must light clouds brighter than the sea. Fit the airglow colour against limb-panorama and airglow-red-yellow (green peak with G > R > B but B about 0.7 R, as photographed), and thin the red layer. Add these to the leo-night-airglow spec: the surface's mean below the band less than 0.3x the band, and a neutral hue for any moonlit cloud.

findings.defect: Item 10 is still open. Clouds between the camera and a setting sun are bright warm tan (175, 154, 135), about 0.8x the glow next to them (224, 197, 150), so the low band reads as a beige haze. The high clouds away from the sun now have pink-tan tops and grey bases, which is better. Looking into a 40 deg sun, the clouds near it are flat mid-grey (131-153) with only a faint brightening at the edges: no silver lining.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/sky-ground-clouds/sunset-crepuscular-pacific.jpg: clouds against the sun are dark silhouettes (50, 50, 46) with bright silver edges, cloud p95/p5 14.7x. low-sun-stratocumulus.jpg: backlit cores (42, 44, 42), rims only a few px wide, about 6x edge to core. cb-sunset-panorama.jpg: only sunward faces glow, shaded parts blue-grey (84, 73, 82).
findings.likelyCause: As the hand-off says, the high-order (multiple-scattering) term is weighted by the reflected share of the two-stream solution, which is isotropic, so a thick cloud seen from its unlit side still glows with reddened sunlight. The forward lobe is not concentrated at the optically thin rim.
findings.fixDirection: On the anti-sun side, weight the high-order term by the transmitted share T(tau), so thick backlit cores go dark. Let the forward Henyey-Greenstein lobe act only where the optical depth toward the eye and the sun is small (rim), and add a sharp silver-lining term there. Spec: in the sunset view, the median of cloud pixels within 20 deg of the sun is under 0.4x the adjacent sky, and edge to core is over 3x.

findings.defect: The blocker is gone: separate clouds, flat grey bases, blue sky between them, tops 5.3x the zenith-side sky. On a second look they are still CGI. The large bodies are smooth and airbrushed, with painted swoosh shading and soft 3-6 px edges against razor-sharp terrain. There is no cauliflower knotting at 1:1. In perf-pad-1440p.png the congestus is a smooth flat-topped loaf with near-vertical sides (top edge within y 481-531 over 450 px). The stratus above it has a sparkly, stippled fringe that looks like dithering, not wisps. Near the horizon the clouds stack into several horizontal shelves at different base heights, like a pile of plates.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/sky-ground-clouds/cu-humilis-nsw.jpg and cu-mediocris.jpg: crisp curled cauliflower edges sharp to the pixel, brilliant tops, bases at one level; rows near the horizon flatten but keep crisp tops. cu-congestus-from-aircraft.jpg: towers made of rounded turrets at every scale, with deep self-shadowed crevices; no flat tops below the tropopause.
findings.likelyCause: The shape noise still lacks a mid octave (150-600 m) with enough amplitude near the camera, and erosion only displaces the surface slightly. The loaf top is the height-dependent threshold closing all shapes at the same profile top. The stippled fringe is per-pixel erosion jitter that the half-resolution buffer and the plain upsample do not resolve.
findings.fixDirection: Add a turret term: a billow octave of Worley (inverted, 200-500 m) weighted toward the upper half of each cloud, so tops are made of domes. Vary the profile top per cloud from a low-frequency field so tops do not share one height. Sharpen the edge ramp, and use an edge-aware upsample guided by alpha and depth. Iterate side by side with cu-humilis-nsw at 1440p.

findings.defect: The cumulus fields over the sea now have tops, sides and shadows and pass at a glance. Three things still read CGI. (1) Far banks are flat-topped horizontal slabs, two or three stacked, with stippled dotted tops and ruler-straight bases running edge to edge, like trimmed hedges. (2) At 5 km a stratiform cloud is a smooth sausage-shaped tube with a fuzzy underside. (3) At 10 km a milky translucent veil with a fine sandpaper stipple lies over the near system on the left. Large systems from 25-40 km are still smooth white masses with no granular texture.
findings.realReference: out/qa/ref/sky-ground-clouds/cu-from-airliner-10km.jpg: lumpy distinct heaps compressing smoothly into a whitish haze band at the horizon, never stacked slabs. earth-orbit-clouds/cb-africa.jpg: cumulus fields below have pebbly texture down to the pixel; an anvil is a smooth plate but with a fibrous edge and a shaded underside.
findings.likelyCause: Far layers are integrated analytically per step (round 1, part 4), which gives each layer a flat top and base when seen edge-on. Nothing gives distant banks a top-height profile. The tube and the veil are stratiform sheets with smooth bell profiles; the veil's stipple is jitter that the deterministic or animated resolve does not converge.
findings.fixDirection: For edge-on far layers, modulate the analytic integration by a mesoscale top-height field per column so banks have lumpy tops and broken bases. Give sheets fibrous horizontal detail and a top relief. Converge or filter the veil. Review at 1440p next to cu-from-airliner-10km.

findings.defect: Previous item 16, raised to major on a fresh look because the camera passes through a deck on every ascent. The frame is one featureless grey card: (122, 123, 129) with sd 1.2 per channel in the deterministic frame, and (143-146, 141-145, 140-148) with sd about 2 in the 1440p animated frame. There is no gradient toward the sun or the top, no texture streaming past, and no sense of motion. The player reads it as an untextured fog shader.
findings.realReference: Cockpit footage flying through cloud: a bright white-out, lighter overhead and toward the sun, with turbulent wisps and density fluctuations streaming past the window and brief brighter and darker pockets. Near the top the sun shows as a diffuse glow. (No still photograph in the library; sky-ground-clouds/overcast-landscape.jpg gives the mottling scale of a deck from below.)
findings.likelyCause: No near-camera density detail: stepMinM 60 m and the finest erosion acts only at the surface. Inside deep cloud, the sample light is a column mean, and the ambient collapses with the large optical depth.
findings.fixDirection: Add a near-camera fog term within about 200 m, with small-scale animated noise advected by the wind and the vessel's velocity. Add a directional glow from forward-scattered sun through the remaining optical depth, and a vertical brightness gradient from the depth below the top. Check against a diffusion estimate. Spec: sd above a floor and a brightness gradient toward the top.

findings.view: Specs (not re-run; screenshots are newer than the last commit to src/render/atmosphere): tests/browser/atmosphere/transparents.spec.ts 'above a broken layer'; atmosphere.perf.spec.ts; clouds.spec.ts 60,000 km
findings.defect: Reported by the fixer and recorded in hand-off section 11; not re-measured here. In transparents.spec.ts, a quad in front of the cloud keeps 0.837 of its brightness against a bound of 0.85: an exhaust plume in front of a cumulus would be wrongly dimmed by cloud behind it. The perf spec fails two atmosphere p99 rows (pad q 1: 0.869 against 0.8; low orbit q 0.7: 5.4 ms). From 60,000 km, the half-resolution buffer that transparents read is less opaque than the shown picture (0.33 against 0.38), so trails seen there will show through cloud.
findings.realReference: Liftoff and ascent photographs (out/qa/ref/liftoff-ascent/): a plume in front of a cloud is unattenuated by it, and a plume behind a cloud is hidden.
findings.likelyCause: clouds.depth puts the cloud's begin nearer than the cloud at that pixel (hand-off). The p99 spikes are in the composite (reported as contention on a loaded machine). The half-resolution buffer is not the fine tile.
findings.fixDirection: Make clouds.depth the depth of the first optical-depth threshold, not a transmittance-weighted mean, where a ray crosses a gap. Publish the fine tile's transmittance for transparents when the tile is in use. Re-measure perf on a quiet machine before accepting.
